extracted.intended_audience: NLP and computational-humour researchers; ML/NLP practitioners interested in humour generation and explanation
extracted.subtask_description: A survey of computational humour focused on generative tasks (creating humour) and explanatory tasks (explaining humour), summarizing the literature, current model limitations, and future research directions that consider subjectivity and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative humour capability (beyond puns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of systems to generate humour across a variety of forms, not limited to puns. The paper observes that work on generating humour beyond puns remains sparse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether models can produce different humour types (e.g., situational, incongruity-based, character-driven) and not only pun-based wordplay; note the literature gap and benchmark against human outputs where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour explanation capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to explain why a piece of text is humorous—i.e., to produce coherent explanations of the mechanisms or knowledge that make a joke funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess explanatory outputs for correctness, completeness, and alignment with human judgments; treat explanation as a generative task distinct from mere classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense knowledge and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which humour creation and understanding require and demonstrate common-sense knowledge and complex reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humour tasks as probes of a model's commonsense and multi-step reasoning abilities; evaluate whether generated humour reflects appropriate background/world knowledge and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependence and situational sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is frequently context-dependent; successful generation and interpretation depend on situational, cultural, and conversational context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure models' ability to condition humour on context and to adapt jokes appropriately to situation and audience; include contextual prompts and varied scenarios in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour perception is subjective—different audiences will find different things funny—so evaluation must account for variability in human judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate diverse human raters, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and analysis of demographic/cultural variation when evaluating humour; avoid single-point gold labels where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical ambiguity and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can be ethically ambiguous; generation systems may produce content that is offensive or harmful if not constrained or evaluated for ethical risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include safety checks, bias/harms evaluations, and ethical risk assessments in both generation and explanation tasks; consider guidelines to avoid producing abusive or discriminatory humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking against human capability
rubrics_metrics.description: State-of-the-art models continue to fall short of human capabilities in creating and explaining humour; comparisons to human performance are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human baselines for both generation quality and explanation accuracy; report gaps and specific failure modes relative to human performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage and taxonomy of humour types
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensiveness of work across different humour types and phenomena—whether research and evaluation cover the landscape of humour phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether datasets, models, and metrics account for a wide taxonomy of humour (puns, sarcasm, irony, satire, slapstick descriptions, etc.) and identify underexplored areas.
